newsitem.title: UK: Stg/mark sets new high, UK budget worry halts rise.
newsitem.headline: Stg/mark sets new high, UK budget worry halts rise.

text.p: Sterling clambered to a new 59-month high against the mark, recovering from a bout of profit-taking as expectations of higher UK interest rates persisted.
The pound was unable to sustain gains above 2.88 marks for long, though, amid concern the Bank of England could intervene to curb sterling's gains.

Traders were also wary of pushing the pound too high before the UK budget next week. The risk is that Chancellor Gordon Brown will tighten fiscal policy by more than traders expect, and reduce the need for rates to rise as far or as quickly as the market is discounting, analysts said.

"The pound can probably go higher, but the market is getting nervous as we approach the budget," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank in London. "People who have made some money on sterling this week are looking to square up before the weekend and won't be putting on new long positions before they see what Brown comes up with."

Sterling rose as high as 2.8825 marks, the strongest it has been since July 1992. The pound was quoted at 2.8764/69 marks at 1425 GMT against 2.8685/95 late Wednesday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6650/60 against $1.6627/37 late yesterday. Sterling's trade-weighted index rose to 101.6 from 101.3 late Wednesday.
Economists polled by Reuters on average expect fiscal policy to be tightened by about 4 billion pounds.
David Bloom, currency strategist at HSBC James Capel here, doesn't expect this will be enough to rein in domestic demand and predicted that the pound would soon resume its climb.

"Given that U.S. rates seem to be on hold for the time being, we look to be the only G7 country to be raising rates on a sustainable basis," he said. "That means people should still be buying sterling."
Sterling has also benefited from expectations a broad range of countries will launch European economic and monetary union.

Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said Thursday there were signs that investors were transferring funds into the perceived safe havens of sterling, the Swiss franc, and the dollar in the run-up to EMU.
Traders said there was no sign that the Bank of England intervened to counter sterling gains Thursday.
Still, they don't expect the UK central bank will allow the pound to continue rallying at the pace it has in recent weeks.
For one thing, sterling strength is hurting one of the most vulnerable parts of the UK economy -- the export sector.
A pick-up in growth elsewhere in Europe will help offset the damage the surging pound has inflicted on UK exporters' competitiveness, according to Bloom at HSBC James Capel.
Still, this will only mask "the current account early warning system" which usually prevents an exchange rate from remaining too overvalued for too long, he said.
